RealityForge

Make a desk respond to what is on it.

A browser prototype that calibrates a planar desk and tracks foreground silhouettes as obstacles for marble collisions, particle avoidance, and creature navigation.

01 / THE QUESTION

What needed to work?

A simple camera and an ordinary desk can become an input surface for a simulation, provided the geometry and perception limits stay explicit.

Planar calibration, foreground tracking, marble and particle interactions, local hand controls, and a clip-annotation evaluation bench.

03 / THE ENGINEERING

The decision behind it.

Work with a calibrated 2D desk and persistent foreground silhouettes. This keeps the prototype practical on a Mac without claiming general 3D reconstruction.

  1. 01Desk calibration
  2. 02Silhouette tracking
  3. 03Hand & gesture controls
  4. 04Interactive simulation
  • Used a planar desk calibration and foreground silhouettes to drive interactive simulations.
  • Added local hand and pinch controls and a session-based personal gesture classifier.
  • Built a clip-annotation evaluation bench.
  • Evaluated segmentation and tracking on six annotated synthetic clips containing 144 frames, including lighting changes, shadows, and hand occlusion.

04 / THE EVIDENCE

What the work demonstrates.

The original app runs a vision worker and responsive simulations. Its preserved evaluation covers synthetic clips; real-camera generalization remains unvalidated.

The included app runs its actual vision worker on synthetic desk frames. The project also preserves evaluation across six annotated synthetic clips and 144 labeled frames.

BOUNDARY OF THE EVIDENCE

Synthetic evaluation does not establish real-camera generalization. The actual app offers optional local camera input; the scene illustration uses synthetic obstacles.

05 / THE BOUNDARIES

What I can stand behind.

Synthetic evaluation does not establish real-camera generalization. The actual app offers optional local camera input; the scene illustration uses synthetic obstacles.

Building something useful means being precise about what it does, what has been checked, and what still needs to be tested.
